 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of medical charts for 25 runners (14 men, 11 women, mean age 29 years) diagnosed with exertional heat stroke at an 11 km road race medical tent. Glasgow Coma Scale scores were compared with rectal temperature, and the authors report a significant but weak negative correlation overall (rs = -0.255, p = 0.004, R2 = 0.06) and no significant correlation when rectal temperature was above 40 C (rs = -0.209, p = 0.108).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The design is a retrospective chart review of 25 patients from one race, and charts were recorded by scribes who did not always document persistent signs between time points. The correlations rely on repeated observations per patient, and the study cannot show whether GCS changes cause cooling decisions.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may take the weak GCS correlation as evidence that mental status can stand in for rectal temperature when cooling, when the authors say it cannot be used to end cold water immersion.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Yeargin SW, Scarneo-Miller SE, Jardine J, Troyanos C, Lopez R. The Association Between Central Nervous System Function and Core Body Temperature in Patients With Exertional Heat Stroke. Clin J Sport Med. 2025;00(00):1-7.",
   "doi":"10.1097/JSM.0000000000001383",
   "abstract":"The study describes central nervous system function using the Glasgow Coma Scale in patients with exertional heat stroke treated at a road race medical tent, and tests whether GCS relates to rectal temperature. The authors find only a weak overall correlation and none above 40 C, and conclude that GCS may not capture CNS dysfunction in this condition.",
   "tldr":"In 25 runners treated for exertional heat stroke, Glasgow Coma Scale scores tracked rectal temperature only weakly and not at the dangerous high temperatures. Rectal temperature should still guide cooling, and mental status alone should not be used to stop it.",
   "methods":"Retrospective cross-sectional review of deidentified medical charts from an 11 km race medical tent. Scribes recorded GCS subscales and cumulative scores at each rectal temperature reading, roughly every 3 minutes, and Spearman correlations were used to test the link between rectal temperature and GCS.",
   "findings":"Of 25 patients (14 men, 11 women, aged 29 plus or minus 13 years), the mean initial rectal temperature was 41.0 plus or minus 0.6 C and the mean cumulative GCS was 14 plus or minus 3 (range 4 to 15). Confusion was the most frequently recorded CNS sign (19.8%). Overall, rectal temperature and GCS had a significant but weak negative correlation (rs = -0.255, p = 0.004, R2 = 0.06). At time points above 40 C, the correlation was not significant (rs = -0.209, p = 0.108), and the Eye, Verbal and Motor subscales were also not significant.",
   "limitations":"Charts were completed during busy care, so some variables were not recorded at every time point, and persistent signs were not always documented. Only patients who reached a station with their own chart were included. The study is from one race with 25 patients, and the authors say a universal GCS guideline cannot be drawn from it.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians should keep using rectal temperature to guide cold water immersion and to decide when to stop cooling, and should not use GCS or mental status to decide when cooling is complete. Where rectal temperature cannot be measured, the authors advise estimating cooling time from the likely core temperature, the body area in water and the water temperature.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The study concerns acute heat illness rather than performance. For staff at endurance events, it reinforces that rectal temperature measurement should be available at the medical tent.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The paper covers acute treatment of exertional heat stroke in race patients and does not address return to sport. It cannot inform return timing or criteria after heat stroke."
 }
}

import json
d=json.load(open('drafts/Q63.json'))
p=d['paper']
old="Glasgow Coma Scale scores were compared with rectal temperature, and"
assert old in d['evidenceSummary']
d['evidenceSummary']=d['evidenceSummary'].replace(old,"In the 22 patients with at least one documented GCS score, Glasgow Coma Scale scores were compared with rectal temperature, and")
old2="The correlations rely on repeated observations per patient, and the study cannot show whether GCS changes cause cooling decisions."
assert old2 in d['screeningLimitations']
d['screeningLimitations']=d['screeningLimitations'].replace(old2,"The correlations pool repeated observations from 22 patients, and the study did not test patient outcomes of GCS-guided versus temperature-guided cooling.")
p['citation']="Yeargin SW, Scarneo-Miller SE, Jardine J, Troyanos C, Lopez R. The Association Between Central Nervous System Function and Core Body Temperature in Patients With Exertional Heat Stroke. Clin J Sport Med. 2025."
p['methods']=p['methods'].replace("and Spearman correlations were used to test the link between rectal temperature and GCS.","and Spearman correlations tested the link between rectal temperature and GCS in the 22 patients with at least one documented GCS score.")
assert "22 patients" in p['methods']
old3="Where rectal temperature cannot be measured, the authors advise estimating cooling time from the likely core temperature, the body area in water and the water temperature."
assert old3 in p['practicalImplications']
p['practicalImplications']=p['practicalImplications'].replace(old3,"Where rectal temperature cannot be measured, the authors suggest estimating cooling time from the likely core temperature, the body area in water and the water temperature, while noting this does not represent best practice.")
d['verification']={"status":"CORRECTED","changes":[
 "evidenceSummary / paper.methods: correlations were not run on all 25 patients -> 22 with at least one documented GCS ('EHS patients with at least 1 documented GCS score (n = 22) were included in correlational analyses')",
 "paper.citation: removed placeholder volume/issue/pages '00(00):1-7' ('Clin J Sport Med 2025;00:1-7'; 'Volume 00 Number 00')",
 "paper.practicalImplications: added the authors' caveat that estimating cooling time without rectal temperature 'does not represent best practice'",
 "screeningLimitations: replaced unclear causal sentence with the pooled-observation and no-outcome-test limits"],
 "residualConcerns":"",
 "spotCheckPriority":"high"}
json.dump(d,open('verified/Q63.json','w'),indent=1,ensure_ascii=False)
EOF
cat drafts/Q64.json

{
 "id":"Q64",
 "sourceFile":"The Association Between Early Sport Specialization and Injury and Career Outcomes Among National Football League Athletes.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title 'The Association Between Early Sport Specialization and Injury and Career Outcomes Among National Football League Athletes' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Coaching"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective cohort of 2,556 male NFL draftees from 2011 to 2023 who played at least 16 career games, classified as multisport or single-sport by high school varsity participation. Multisport athletes (about 64%) had lower total and major injury incidence rate ratios than single-sport athletes (IRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.85; major IRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.82, both p less than 0.001), and played 12.2 more NFL games (95% CI 9.2 to 15.1) and 0.7 more career years (95% CI 0.5 to 0.9).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The design is retrospective and observational, with classification and injury data taken from public records and media, and models were not adjusted for age or other player characteristics. Only injuries leading to missed games or injured-reserve designation were captured, and the cohort is elite, male and drafted, so the findings may not apply to youth players.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may read the multisport advantage as proof that early football specialization causes injury or shorter careers, when the authors state that differences in athleticism or coaching could explain the association.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2026,
   "citation":"Chundi G, Dawar A, Fuller Z, Jones T, Lingam S, Galdi B. The Association Between Early Sport Specialization and Injury and Career Outcomes Among National Football League Athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2026;26:e70120.",
   "doi":"10.1002/ejsc.70120",
   "abstract":"The study tested whether playing only football in high school is associated with higher injury rates and shorter NFL careers than multisport participation. Among NFL draftees from 2011 to 2023, multisport athletes had fewer total and major injuries per 1000 snaps and longer careers.",
   "tldr":"Among NFL draftees, those who played several sports in high school had fewer injuries per snap and longer careers than those who played only football. The result is an association from observational data, so it does not show that early specialization causes harm.",
   "methods":"Retrospective cohort of NFL players drafted 2011 to 2023 who played at least 16 career games, excluding kickers and punters. High school sport history came from public records and injury data from online databases. Injury rates per 1000 snaps were compared using position-stratified incidence rate ratios, with false discovery rate correction for position analyses.",
   "findings":"Of 2,556 players, about 64% were multisport athletes. Multisport athletes had lower total injury incidence (IRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.85) and major injury incidence (IRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.82), both p less than 0.001. They played 12.2 more NFL games (95% CI 9.2 to 15.1) and had 0.7 more career years (95% CI 0.5 to 0.9). The authors report the injury advantage was most evident in several position groups, including defensive backs.",
   "limitations":"The retrospective design cannot establish causation, and the authors note that athleticism or coaching quality could explain both specialization and durability. Classification and injury reporting may be incomplete, minor in-play injuries were not captured, and models were not adjusted for age or other player characteristics. The cohort is male, elite and drafted only, and the authors note that definitions of early specialization vary across the literature.",
   "practicalImplications":"Youth football programmes and families can use these results to support multisport participation in high school, since the study links it with fewer injuries and longer careers. Staff should not use the result to claim that early football specialization directly causes injury, because the study cannot separate it from athlete and coaching differences.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The findings support encouraging young football players to take part in other sports, since multisport history was linked with longer professional careers and more games played. The study does not measure performance itself.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study covers injury incidence and career length in professional players, not rehabilitation or return from a specific injury. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}
